title: Where is the Sun ever straight up?
hook: The Sun climbs highest at noon. Where does it ever stand straight overhead?

knows: that the Sun is high in summer in hot places
that latitude measures distance from the equator
doesNotKnow: where on Earth the Sun can ever be exactly overhead
that the tropics are set by the Earth's tilt

misconception: The Sun is directly overhead in summer in places like Florida or Texas.
objective: The learner can say that the noon Sun is only ever overhead between about 23.4 degrees north and south, because that is the tilt of the Earth's axis.

claims.text: The noon Sun is overhead only between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, about 23.4 degrees north and south, set by the Earth's tilt of about 23.4 degrees.
claims.source: Obliquity of the ecliptic about 23.44 degrees (IAU 2006; Astronomical Almanac), drifting about 0.013 degrees per century. The Sun's declination ranges over +/- obliquity. From memory, not checked online.

claims.text: City latitudes: Honolulu 21.3 N, Miami 25.8 N, Cairo 30.0 N.
claims.source: Gazetteer coordinates from memory (GeoNames-style: Honolulu 21.31 N 157.86 W, Miami 25.76 N 80.19 W, Cairo 30.04 N 31.24 E); not checked online. Drawn as markers, not as kit data (Honolulu is not in the 1:110m shapes).

claims.text: The noon Sun passes over Honolulu on about 27 May and again on about 16 July.
claims.source: Days nearest 21.31 N in Demo.tsx's declination model (Kepler orbit, e = 0.0167, perihelion 3 Jan, Sun longitude at perihelion 282.94 degrees, obliquity 23.44): day 147 (21.31) and day 197 (21.35) in a non-leap year. The brief's sine formula gives the same days. Real dates shift by a day with the year; the lesson says 'about'. NOAA Solar Calculator not consulted. | v2: sentence no longer shown to learners; withdrawn.

claims.text: The overhead noon Sun reaches its farthest north, 23.4 N, around 21 June, which is farther north than Honolulu (21.3 N) and short of Miami and Cairo.
claims.source: Maximum of the model's declination: 23.44 on day 172 (21 June). The June solstice falls on 20 or 21 June in current years (any almanac). | v2 (2026-10-14): claim text rewritten to match the revised stage; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): Node with the Demo.tsx Kepler model: maximum declination 23.440 on day 172 = 21 June (non-leap), dateLabel '21 Jun', fmtLat '23.4N'. 23.4 > 21.31 (Honolulu) and < 25.76 (Miami), 30.04 (Cairo). Matches the reveal.

claims.text: Outside the tropics, even on the longest day, the noon Sun stays a little short of straight up.
claims.source: Noon solar elevation = 90 - |latitude - declination|; it reaches 90 only where |latitude| <= the maximum declination.

claims.text: Latitude is how far north or south of the equator a place is.
claims.source: Standard definition of geographic latitude. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): The claim text is right, but the stage says something else: the caption under the map reads 'Latitude is how far north of the equator a place is.', which omits south while the same stage draws and labels the Tropic of Capricorn at 23.4S. Fix (builder, Demo.tsx caption): 'Latitude is how far north or south of the equator a place is.' Re-check after the edit. | v3 (2026-10-14): text/stage revised after fact-check pass; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Re-check after v3: Demo.tsx caption now reads 'Latitude is how far north or south of the equator a place is.' Pass 17 dispute resolved.

recall.question: A city sits at 24.5 N. Is the noon Sun ever straight overhead there?
options: No, it is just outside the tropics
recall.why: The overhead Sun never goes farther north than the Tropic of Cancer at about 23.4 N, the Earth's tilt. 24.5 N is just beyond it.
